questions.q: According to this lesson, why is an environment that only one engineer understands a real liability, even if it currently runs fine?
options: Because that knowledge disappears the moment that person is unavailable, and fixes that should be quick become slow and risky
Because monitoring tools refuse to work on undocumented resources
Because cloud providers charge extra for undocumented resources
Because it is not actually a liability as long as nothing breaks
questions.explain: The risk isn't that the environment breaks — it's that when it does, the only person who could fix it quickly isn't there, turning a 20-minute fix into days.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by treating documentation as part of the 'definition of done'?
options: Documentation is optional once the environment passes its smoke test
Definition of done applies only to application code, never to infrastructure
Only customer-facing documentation counts as 'done'
A deployment isn't finished when it's running — it's finished when someone other than the builder could understand and safely operate it
questions.explain: The lesson sets a higher bar than 'it works': done means operable and understandable by someone besides the person who built it.

questions.q: What is a 'bus factor' of 1, as used in this lesson?
options: A rating of how reliable a cloud region is
A metric that counts how many buses connect to a network
A measurement of how many backups an environment has
A situation where only one person could leave or become unavailable before the team loses the ability to operate something
questions.explain: Bus factor describes how fragile a team's operational knowledge is — a bus factor of 1 means a single unavailable person creates a real gap.

options: The gap between what an environment actually does and what's actually written down about it, which compounds like technical debt until something forces a reckoning
Money owed to a cloud provider for storing documentation files
A term with no real meaning used only loosely by teams
A penalty applied by monitoring tools to undocumented resources
questions.explain: Like technical debt, documentation debt accumulates quietly and gets collected at the worst time — usually during an incident.

questions.q: What is the 'six-month test' described in this lesson?
options: A test run automatically by the cloud provider every six months
Asking whether someone else on the team could answer basic questions about the environment without the original builder, after six months have passed
A rule that documentation older than six months must be deleted
A requirement that every resource be redeployed every six months
questions.explain: The six-month test is a gut check: if the builder were unreachable, could anyone else answer why things are configured the way they are?
